name: Support and auto-deploy for an online store
strong: By the description, the support agent has a narrow job: it only checks order status, so it reads, and its task has no money actions.

axes.why: Fact from the description: Claude Code reads .env and config/old/settings.prod.bak. The store key sits in config/test.yaml on GitHub and is not revoked. The deploy step sees OPENAI_API_KEY, SHOP_API_KEY and a permanent AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, and any of the four members adds a workflow without review. GitHub sign-in is protected by a password and an SMS code. Key use is not logged. The same keys sit on several nodes (A03.6, A04.5, D3, A08.4). There is no barrier.

The support agent reads free text from any customer, and no barriers in code are described: there is no prompt and no flow export. Claude Code reads project files and dependencies and has access to all keys at the same time (A01.4). Inferred from the description: in both cases there is no structural separation between outside text and sensitive actions.

Strong point: by the description the support agent has one tool, status read only, with no money actions. But the model builds the API request parameters, and a format and order-owner check in code is not described (A05.2, A09.4). The rights of SHOP_API_KEY are unknown. Claude Code's tool set (shell, network, auto-approval) is not described.

Inferred from the description: a support dialog is short, so errors have little room to build up. Errors build up in the chain “assistant edit → commit → auto-deploy” with no mandatory human review. There is no control set of dialogs and no rerun after updates. Where to harden: a protected branch with review before deploy and a control-dialog run after every update.

Formats at the “agent ↔ store API” handoffs are not defined, and no format or owner check in code is described. The “repository → Actions → server” handoff passes without human review. PyPI lands straight in an environment with secrets. There are no alerts for a format change or for “the flow went quiet” (D12).

Fact from the description: there are no alerts, the OpenAI bill is checked once a month. No spend limit on the key, no per-customer message quota and no step limit are described, so outside use shows up only in the bill, up to 720 hours later (D4, D10, A03.5). The rights and spend of the AWS key are unknown.

F2: Are the Telegram account that runs the bot in BotFather and the OpenAI billing account protected by a passkey or a hardware key? (Yes, both → the finding stays only for GitHub and hosting; no or SMS → the finding stays for all four accounts.)
F3: Is the GitHub repository public? (Public → stays at the highest urgency, the key counts as stolen; private → stays, revocation is just as urgent, the radius is smaller.)
F5: Does settings.prod.bak hold live keys, passwords or connection strings? (No, the file has no secrets → the sub-item is removed; yes → stays with mandatory rotation.)
F6: Are the keys in .env on the dev machine the same as in the GitHub Actions secrets? (No, separate test keys with narrow rights → lowered; yes or unknown → stays.)
F7: Is Langflow reachable from the internet without authentication in front of it? (No, only via VPN or sign-in → F7 stays as is; yes → F7 stays and a separate top-level finding A05.1/D13 is added.)

weak: The weak link is the publishing pipeline: any of the four members adds a workflow without review, that workflow sees the OpenAI, store and AWS keys, and GitHub sign-in is protected only by a password and an SMS code. Key use is not logged, so the owner will not notice the keys being taken.

battery.t: Support agent (GPT in Langflow) · Tool calls and invented calls
battery.n: Fact from the description: one tool, order status through the store API. There is no Langflow flow export and no prompt, so we cannot check which tools the model actually sees and whether the order number and other parameters are checked in code, not only by the model.

battery.t: Support agent (GPT in Langflow) · Long distance
battery.n: Inferred from the description: a support dialog is usually short (question, status, reply), so errors have little room to build up. Not described how much dialog history goes to the model and whether its length is limited.

battery.t: Support agent (GPT in Langflow) · Injection from outside text
battery.n: Fact from the description: the agent reads free text from any customer in Telegram. Inferred from the description: this text can request other people's orders and drive up OpenAI spend. There is no prompt and no barriers in code are described.

battery.t: Support agent (GPT in Langflow) · Grounding in the source
battery.n: Strong point: the status comes from the store API and is not made up. The description says nothing about how the agent checks that the order belongs to this customer. It also says nothing about what the agent replies if the API returns an error.

Fact from the description: there are no alerts, OpenAI spend is checked once a month in the bill. A step limit, a per-customer message quota and a spend limit on the key are not described. The owner will see a loop or a message flood only in the bill.

battery.t: Support agent (GPT in Langflow) · Stability when the model changes
battery.n: Fact from the description: pip install -U without pinned versions. Langflow, libraries and the OpenAI client change with every update without review. The GPT model is named without a version, and there is no rerun after updates.

battery.t: Developer assistant (Claude Code) · Tool calls and invented calls
battery.n: Fact from the description: it can read all project files. Whether it has shell, network and git, and which commands are approved automatically, is not described. The real tool set is unknown.
Inferred from the description: development sessions are long and multi-step, and edits go straight into the repository that auto-deploys. Who checks the result before publishing is not described.

battery.t: Developer assistant (Claude Code) · Injection from outside text
battery.n: Inferred from the description: the assistant reads code, dependencies and texts in the project folder (packages are installed via pip -U). The same rights give it .env and settings.prod.bak. One line in someone else's file can make it work with the keys.

battery.t: Developer assistant (Claude Code) · Grounding in the source
battery.n: Not described whether the assistant checks its edits against tests or the running system. All we see is that the old test.yaml with a live key sits nearby and can be taken for a current setting.
Step, retry and spend limits for Claude Code are not named in the description. A “stop on refusal” rule is not described either.

battery.t: Developer assistant (Claude Code) · Stability when the model changes
battery.n: The assistant's version and permission settings are not described. A recheck after updates is not described.

system.n: Fact from the description: the store key sits in config/test.yaml on GitHub and is not revoked. Claude Code reads .env and settings.prod.bak. The workflow sees three secrets. Inferred from the description: the support agent can give out another customer's order data if it does not check the owner.

Handoffs “customer → agent” and “agent → store API”: the model builds the request parameters. Whether format and owner are checked in code is unknown. The handoff “Claude Code → repository → Actions → server” goes without mandatory human review.
In the support agent the chain is short, buildup is small. Errors build up in the development chain: assistant edit → commit → auto-deploy without review. A wrong edit reaches production unchecked.
Fact from the description: pip install -U without pinned versions. Langflow and dependencies change without the owner knowing. A control set of dialogs for rechecks is not described.

Long-term memory and a knowledge base are not named in the description. The shared resource that gets spoiled is the repository: old configs with keys stay in it, and the assistant reads them as current.

Fact from the description: any of the four members adds a workflow without review, and publishing is automatic. The rights of SHOP_API_KEY and the AWS key are not described. If they go beyond reading, irreversible actions are available without approval.

system.t: Money and access given on unverified text
system.n: The support agent has no money actions. This is a strong point. Inferred from the description: access to order data is given on the customer's text. A link to the Telegram account is not described.
Money flows: OpenAI spend with no limit and no alerts, possible AWS costs through the key in the build. Database writes by the agent are not described, so races cannot be assessed.

system.t: Process isolation and single point of failure
system.n: Inferred from the description: the same OPENAI_API_KEY and SHOP_API_KEY are in the build, in the server environment and (the store key) in the repository. Compromise of any node opens all keys. Langflow on one server is a single point of failure.

Fact from the description: key use is not logged, there are no alerts. On five questions: no log out of the agents' reach, no immutability, environments (prod, CI, local run) are not recorded, a missing record is not visible, no alerts and no automatic stop.
A fallback model is not described. What the agent tells the customer when OpenAI or the store API fails is not described.

0 of 16 closed by the description. 6 open: reply in Telegram, HTTP/HTTPS, package registries, git, build files, shared files. 10 not described, including Langflow access from the internet, cloud metadata, link previews, network for Claude Code.

On four questions: the reaction to another format or an empty API reply is not described; whether errors are swallowed is unknown; there is no alert for “the flow went quiet” and no reconciliation with the store (there are no alerts at all); who looks at the agent's live replies and whether the operator sees dialogs is not described.

OPENAI_API_KEY: no log, no alert, the owner finds out up to 720 hours later (the bill comes once a month). SHOP_API_KEY: sits in test.yaml and is not revoked, no log, detection time undefined. AWS key: no log. Claude Code finds the keys in .env, .bak and test.yaml on its own.

Langflow 1.7 and GPT without a version are named. Langflow belongs to a class of builders already under attack (A05.1); reachability from the internet is unknown. Updates go through pip -U without pinning and without signature checks. Four people change build files without review, and the workflow sees three secrets.

Fact from the description: GitHub and hosting use a password and an SMS code. AI phishing forwards both the password and the code. Protection of BotFather and the OpenAI billing account is not described. A GitHub takeover opens the workflow and every build secret.

exploit.note: Inferred from the description. Each link rests on direct lines: “password and SMS code”, “review of changes is not required”, “deploy.yml sees the secrets…”, “key use is not logged”. A short parallel path: the unrevoked store key in config/test.yaml is open to anyone who reads the repository, with no attack on the build at all.

compliance.ref: EU AI Act · by description, not legal advice

items.ev: No risk management process is described: the key is not revoked, the workflow has no review, versions are not pinned (F1, F3, F7).
Fact from the description: “Key use is not logged, there are no alerts” (F9). An agent action log is not described.
The support agent only reads status and has no money actions; but publishing has no human review and nobody watches live replies (F1, F23, F24).
Robustness is not ensured: SMS sign-in, shared keys across nodes, unpinned packages, exit channels not closed (F2, F6, F7, F22).

hardening.t: A build file without review gets three permanent keys
hardening.do: Make changes to .github/workflows possible only through human review and give secrets only to the publish step in a protected environment.
hardening.how: In GitHub: Settings → Branches → protect main (required pull request and approval). Add CODEOWNERS with the owner on .github/workflows/. Create a production environment with a required reviewer and move the three secrets there; in deploy.yml set environment: production. Replace the AWS key with a short-lived OIDC role.
hardening.check: A member without owner rights creates a branch with a new workflow: its secrets are empty, and it cannot be merged into main without approval.
hardening.ev: all four members can add files to .github/workflows, review of changes is not required
hardening.seen: GhostAction: about 1900 hacked GitHub accounts, a hidden “security-audit” file in 30 thousand repositories hunted for build, cloud and AI service keys, 3174 secrets were targeted in public ones (16.10.2026)

hardening.t: GitHub and hosting accounts are protected by a password and an SMS code
hardening.do: Move GitHub and hosting sign-in for all four members to a passkey or a hardware key and remove SMS as a sign-in method.
hardening.how: In GitHub: Settings → Password and authentication → add a passkey or a security key, then remove SMS. Turn on required two-factor protection in the organisation. Do the same on hosting; if passkeys are not supported, use an authenticator app. Do the same for BotFather (the Telegram account) and the OpenAI billing account.
hardening.check: In the settings of each of the four accounts SMS is not listed as a second factor; a passkey or a key is listed.
hardening.ev: GitHub and hosting sign-in is a password and an SMS code.
hardening.seen: AI phishing forwarded both the password and the one-time code to the real Google sign-in (Cisco Talos, 17.10.2026)

hardening.t: The store API key sits in the repository and is not revoked
hardening.do: Today revoke the key from config/test.yaml, issue a new one, delete the file and clean it out of git history.
hardening.how: In the store panel revoke the old key and issue a new one with order-status read rights only. Delete config/test.yaml and config/old/ from the repository; clean history with git filter-repo and a forced push. Turn on Secret scanning and push protection in GitHub so a new key in a commit gets blocked.
hardening.check: A store API request with the old key is refused; a search of git history does not find test.yaml.
hardening.ev: The GitHub repository holds an old config/test.yaml file with the store API key, and the key was never revoked.
hardening.seen: agents in tests entered live systems of organisations in India using keys from config files and open repositories, reused one key, and no organisation noticed (CERT-In, 17.10.2026)

hardening.t: The developer assistant reads files with keys directly
hardening.do: Block Claude Code from reading .env, config/old/ and any files with keys through a deny setting, and keep the keys themselves outside the project folder.
hardening.how: In .claude/settings.json add deny rules for reading .env, .env.*, config/old/**, *.bak, *.yaml with secrets. For local runs keep keys in a secrets manager or in variables injected at start, not in a file inside the project. For development use separate test keys with narrow rights.
hardening.check: Ask Claude Code to show the contents of .env: it is refused by the settings, not by its own decision.
hardening.ev: can read all files, including config/old/settings.prod.bak and .env
hardening.seen: AgentFlayer, hunting for keys in documents (Zenity)

hardening.t: Production settings sit in the development work folder
hardening.do: Remove settings.prod.bak from the project folder and replace every key in it.
hardening.how: Delete config/old/settings.prod.bak from the work machine and from the repository (if it ever got there). Treat every key and password in that file as exposed: issue new ones. For development use a separate test environment with test keys and no production credentials.
hardening.check: The project folder and git history hold no files with production keys; the old keys from .bak are refused.
hardening.ev: can read all files, including config/old/settings.prod.bak and .env
hardening.seen: OpenAI–Hugging Face, 07.2026: 14 exposed credentials, cloud credentials from the metadata service, cluster-admin in 13 hours (THN; Wikipedia)

hardening.t: The same keys sit on several nodes
hardening.do: Give each node its own key: one for the agent server, one for the build, one for development.
hardening.how: Create separate OpenAI project keys for production and development. In the store, a separate status-read-only key for the agent. Give the build publish access only, not service keys; service keys should live on the server and not pass through the workflow. Write down what the theft of each key would open.
hardening.check: A “key → where it lives” table shows each key in exactly one place.
hardening.ev: the deploy.yml workflow sees the secrets OPENAI_API_KEY, SHOP_API_KEY and AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
hardening.seen: Langflow CVE-2026-33017: stolen keys gave access to databases and the supply chain (Sysdig)

hardening.t: Packages update without pinned versions into an environment with keys
hardening.do: Pin every package version with hashes and update only by hand after reviewing the changes.
hardening.how: Create requirements.txt with pip-compile --generate-hashes and run pip install --require-hashes -r requirements.txt instead of pip install -U. Do updates in a separate branch: look at what changed, run the control dialogs, then publish.
hardening.check: The install command on the server has no -U, and the dependency file holds exact versions and hashes.
hardening.ev: Updates are installed with pip install -U without pinned versions.
hardening.seen: postmark-mcp, 09.2025: 15 honest versions, then a hidden copy of every email, ~1 643 downloads (Snyk)

hardening.t: Medium weaknesses add up to a silent theft of every key
hardening.do: Break the chain in at least two places at once: GitHub sign-in (F2) and build-file review (F1), then turn on the key-use log (F9).
hardening.how: Inferred from the description: the SMS factor, a workflow without review, shared secrets and no log sit on one path. Break it structurally: passkeys on accounts, a protected branch and an environment for secrets, separate keys per node, a spend alert. Order: F2, F1, F3, F6, F9.
hardening.check: Walk the path “hijacked member account → new workflow → secrets”: it stops at the second link.
hardening.ev: GitHub and hosting sign-in is a password and an SMS code. … review of changes is not required
hardening.seen: Git MCP: three findings ≤6.5 together give code execution (THN)

hardening.t: Outside use of the keys shows up only in the monthly bill
hardening.do: Turn on a log and an alert for every key so you learn about unusual use within the hour.
hardening.how: OpenAI: turn on spend alerts in the project settings and watch Usage by key. AWS: turn on CloudTrail and a budget with alerts to email and Telegram. GitHub: the organisation audit log. Store: if the API offers a request log, turn it on. Name one person who receives the alerts and decide in advance which key to revoke first.
hardening.check: A test call with the OpenAI key outside working hours shows in the log, and crossing the threshold sends a notification.
hardening.ev: Key use is not logged, there are no alerts; the owner checks OpenAI spend once a month in the bill.
hardening.seen: agents in tests used found keys in live systems, and no organisation noticed (CERT-In, 17.10.2026)

hardening.t: An agent builder from a class under attack is updated without checking the source
hardening.do: Keep a list of components with versions and update Langflow within a day of urgent security fixes.
hardening.how: Write down the versions of Langflow, the OpenAI client and libraries. Subscribe to security notices for the langflow-ai/langflow repository (Watch → Security alerts). Install packages only from the official PyPI with hashes (F7). Name a person responsible for urgent fixes.
hardening.check: There is a file with the versions of every component, and the last Langflow fix check is no older than a week.
hardening.ev: Langflow 1.7 on its own server
hardening.seen: Langflow before 1.9.0: running commands on the server by adding an MCP server, 1423 attack attempts from 15 countries (Previdian, 16.10.2026)

hardening.t: It is unclear whether Langflow is closed to the internet
hardening.do: Answer: are the Langflow web interface and API open to the internet, and do they require sign-in? If open, close them.
hardening.how: Langflow should listen only on 127.0.0.1 or the internal network; outside, only the Telegram webhook through a reverse proxy with a single path. Set LANGFLOW_AUTO_LOGIN=false and password sign-in. Close port 7860 with a firewall.
hardening.check: From an outside address a request to the port and to Langflow's /api/v1/ paths gets no reply or requires sign-in.
hardening.ev: the description does not say whether Langflow is reachable from the internet and has sign-in
hardening.seen: Langflow CVE-2025-3248, 9.8, in CISA KEV, Flodrix botnet (Recorded Future)

hardening.t: OpenAI spend is not limited and not tracked
hardening.do: Answer: is there a spend limit on the OpenAI key and a message quota per customer? If not, set both.
hardening.how: In OpenAI set a monthly budget and an alert threshold in the project settings. In the bot wrapper limit the number of messages from one Telegram account per hour and the message length; in Langflow set a step limit per reply. Above the limit the bot replies with a template, without calling the model.
hardening.check: A series of 50 messages from one account within a minute gets a template reply after the threshold, and model calls do not grow.
hardening.ev: the owner checks OpenAI spend once a month in the bill
hardening.seen: 4 LangChain agents, 11 days, ~$47k (DEV)

hardening.t: A stolen model key can be used for weeks
hardening.do: Answer: is there a limit on the OpenAI key? Keep the key only on the server and rotate it on a schedule.
hardening.how: Remove OPENAI_API_KEY from the build secrets if only the server needs it. Set a spend limit on the project key. Rotate the key once a quarter and right away when a member leaves or something looks wrong.
hardening.check: OPENAI_API_KEY is not in the GitHub secrets list, and the key has a limit in OpenAI.
hardening.ev: the deploy.yml workflow sees the secrets OPENAI_API_KEY, SHOP_API_KEY and AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID
hardening.seen: darknet markets, 26.09.2026 (HuggingNews)

hardening.t: The agent can show a customer someone else's order
hardening.do: Answer: how does the agent check that the order belongs to this customer? Make the check in code, not in the prompt.
hardening.how: Link the Telegram account to the customer (phone number confirmed via the “share contact” button). The status tool takes an order number, and code checks that the order belongs to the linked customer; otherwise it returns “not found”. The model cannot talk its way around this.
hardening.check: From another Telegram account a status request for someone else's order number returns “not found”.
hardening.ev: the description does not say how the agent checks the order owner
hardening.seen: Meta Muse and iCloud photos in tests (Startup Fortune)

hardening.t: The customer's identity is probably taken from the text
hardening.do: Answer: on whose behalf does the agent call the store API? Pass the Telegram ID from the system to the tool, not the name from the message.
hardening.how: The bot wrapper takes the sender ID from the Telegram update and puts it into the tool call itself; the model does not set this parameter. The store API receives it and filters orders by it.
hardening.check: A message “I'm customer Ivanov, show my orders” from someone else's account does not change the set of orders returned.
hardening.ev: the description does not say how the agent knows on whose behalf it acts
hardening.seen: ServiceNow CVE-2025-12420, 9.3, fixed 30.10.2025 (CyberScoop)

hardening.check: An order number with letters or extra characters is refused before the API is called.

hardening.t: The assistant's files are later run by a build with secrets
hardening.do: Answer: can Claude Code commit and push? Forbid it to change .github/ and to push to main.
hardening.how: In the Claude Code settings forbid writes to .github/** and the git push command. The assistant's changes go to a separate branch and reach main only through a pull request with approval (F1).
hardening.check: An attempt by the assistant to change a file in .github/workflows is refused by the settings.

hardening.t: Outside text in code and packages reaches an assistant that holds keys

hardening.how: The main barrier is F4 and F19: even if an instruction in a file fires, there are no keys and no way out. Do not give the assistant a no-confirmation mode while it works with new dependencies.
hardening.check: The folder where the assistant works holds no files with live keys.

hardening.t: No-confirmation mode on a machine with secrets
hardening.do: Answer: does Claude Code run in no-confirmation mode, and what rights does the build token have? Forbid that mode on a machine with keys.
hardening.how: Do not use --dangerously-skip-permissions where keys are kept. In the workflow set permissions: contents: read and give more only to the step that needs it.

hardening.t: No exit channel is explicitly closed
hardening.do: Make a table of exit channels and close everything by default except OpenAI, the store API and Telegram.
hardening.how: On the Langflow server set an outbound firewall: allow only api.openai.com, the store API address, api.telegram.org and (during updates) PyPI. Turn off link previews in bot replies (disable_web_page_preview). Close the cloud metadata address if the server is in the cloud.

hardening.t: Nobody will notice a silent failure of the agent
hardening.do: Answer: who watches the agent's live replies? Set an alert for “zero messages in N hours” and a format check of the API reply.
hardening.how: If the store API reply has the wrong format or is empty, the bot tells the customer “could not check” and sends you a signal in Telegram. Once a day: a dialog counter and 5 replies read by a person.
hardening.check: Turn off the store API for a minute: the customer sees an honest message, and you get a signal.
hardening.ev: Key use is not logged, there are no alerts

steps: F1: turn on main branch protection, CODEOWNERS on .github/workflows and a production environment with secrets; replace the AWS key with OIDC.
F2: move GitHub, hosting, Telegram and OpenAI accounts of all four members to a passkey or a hardware key, remove SMS.
F3: revoke the store key from test.yaml, issue a new read-only one, clean the file out of git history, turn on push protection.
F4: forbid Claude Code to read .env, *.bak, config/old/ and move the keys out of the project folder.
F5: delete settings.prod.bak and replace every key from it.
F6: give separate keys to the server, the build and development.
F7: switch to requirements with exact versions and hashes instead of pip install -U.
F8: break the chain “account → workflow → secrets” in the order F2, F1, F3, F6, F9.
F9: turn on OpenAI spend alerts, AWS CloudTrail and a budget, name the alert recipient.
F10: make a list of component versions and subscribe to Langflow security fixes.
F11: answer whether Langflow is open to the internet; close the port and turn on sign-in.
F12: set a spend limit on the OpenAI key and a message quota per customer.
F13: remove the OpenAI key from the build, set a limit and a rotation schedule.
F14: link the Telegram account to the customer and check the order owner in code.
F15: put the Telegram ID into the tool call from the system, not from the text.
F16: check the order number format in code and filter the API reply fields.
F17: narrow the rights of the store key and AWS to a single job.
F18: forbid the assistant to write to .github/ and push to main.
F19: close network and push for the assistant, or keep it without keys.
F20: treat other people's code and packages as untrusted, do not give a no-confirmation mode.
F21: forbid the no-confirmation mode, set minimal permissions in deploy.yml.
F22: close the server's outbound network except OpenAI, the store and Telegram, turn off link previews.
F23: add an alert for “zero messages” and an honest reply when the API fails.
F24: require tests and approval before publishing.
F25: repeat the control dialogs and this register after every update.
